21.0.s.en: 1. A gentle address to his friends

21.0.0.en: 1 But Job answered and said, 2 Hear diligently my speech, and let this be your consolations. 3 Suffer me that I may speak; and after that I have spoken, mock on. 4 As for me, is my complaint to man? and if it were so, why should not my spirit be troubled? 5 Mark me, and be astonished, and lay your hand upon your mouth.

21.1.0.en: Hear diligently my speech, and let this be your consolations [2].

21.1.1.en: Job begs his friends to listen to him in a spirit of love, and to set their minds on understanding his intentions instead of judging him hastily. He now speaks in the language of friendship and calm, considering that their consolation of him in the midst of his sufferings is their listening to him with a good spirit. Perhaps he also means that as they listen to him thus, he finds rest, and so they are comforted, and by his consolation they are comforted and find rest. As though their listening had a double benefit, for him and for them.

21.1.2.en: Truly, listening to the words of the suffering benefits both sides. On one side the sufferer feels the tenderness of his brethren and their sharing with him, even if only by listening. On the other side, when the sufferer finds rest, his brethren are comforted by his rest, at least to certain degrees.

21.1.3.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that the suffering Church, in the person of Job, calls the heretics and the people of the world to listen to her words, for she is able, through her crucified Christ, to offer them, through sufferings borne with thanksgiving, surpassing divine consolations. St. Paul directs the eyes of the suffering to the cross of the Lord of glory Jesus, not only that they may be filled with consolation, but that they may become a source of consolation to others. He says: "Who comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God" (2 Cor 1:4), and also: "As ye are partakers of the sufferings, so shall ye be also of the consolation" (2 Cor 1:7).

21.1.4.en: The suffering Church imitates our crucified Christ, for having suffered, being tempted, He is able to succour them that are tempted (Heb 2:18). And as we abide in Him we enjoy the fellowship of His sufferings, and are crucified with Him, that we may become through Him a source of unceasing consolations.

21.1.5.en: * Paul rejoices in his sufferings, seeing the wonderful fruits that sufferings bring about in the people, such as the Christians of Corinth.

21.2.0.en: St. John Chrysostom Suffer me that I may speak; and after that I have spoken, mock on! [3]

21.2.1.en: He asked them not to interrupt him in his speech and to bear with his words; then, if they wish, let them mock him as they please. He says this hoping that their listening with a sincere intention will make them receive his words and be convinced by his arguments, and so change their tone.

21.2.2.en: What occupied Job's mind was not his friends' mockery of him, but that they should listen to him and bear with his words for their salvation, edification and consolation. So also the Church is not occupied with her temporal honor or with justifying herself, but what occupies her is the salvation of every soul, even of her opponents and persecutors. For love does not seek its own, but what belongs to others.

21.2.3.en: * It is clear that when someone counsels another and at the same time suffers more than the one he rebukes, he does this not to cause grief to the other, but to offer him deep love. Whereas he who reproves another without this feeling in fact tramples with his feet on his brother's feelings.

21.2.4.en: Fr. Ambrosiaster * Here (2 Cor 1:4) Paul shows that he suffers no less than those who sinned, but more than they. It is very hard for him to bear the pain of the error of the Corinthians that has overtaken him.

21.2.5.en: St. John Chrysostom * The mark of the Church, like her Bridegroom, is true, practical love, whereby she desires, if possible, that the whole world enjoy fellowship in eternal glory.

21.2.6.en: The mockery of people cannot crush the believer or harm the mockers themselves; yet in a spirit of humility Job speaks, asking them to bear with him, that he may win them for God, and they turn back from harming themselves.

21.2.7.en: The Psalmist bore the mockery of the proud, which could not shake his depths so that he turned aside from the law of God, for he says: "The proud have had me greatly in derision: yet have I not declined from thy law" (Ps 119:51). Wisdom cries out saying: "How long, ye simple ones, will ye love simplicity? and the scorners delight in their scorning, and fools hate knowledge?" (Prov 1:22). So she joined the foolish with the scorners and the fools in one class, since all of them acquire destruction for themselves. And the wise man affirms: "If thou be wise, thou shalt be wise for thyself: but if thou scornest, thou alone shalt bear it" (Prov 9:12).

21.2.8.en: And it is wonderful that in the midst of their rebellion against him he speaks in a spirit of meekness and humility, begging them to bear with his words; for his part, he will accept every mockery directed at him, but for the benefit of both sides he asks them to keep calm.

21.2.9.en: *As though he says: "Consider me wicked. But I have gained nothing from these remarks, and I know that you mock me. In any case, I do not give in." He says: "Why? Does a man mock me?" This means that no man can rebuke me, for I am not wrestling with a man!

21.2.10.en: St. John Chrysostom Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that Job's begging his friends to bear with his words is because when he speaks he utters what is for his benefit as well as theirs, if they are willing. He does not speak from the teacher's chair, but from the midst of the dunghill, perhaps to find benefit for himself while he speaks in a quiet spirit in an atmosphere of calm!

21.2.11.en: *When the righteous speak, they observe two things in their speech: that it be for their own benefit and that of their hearers, or for their own alone if it cannot be for the benefit of the hearers. When the good things they utter are heard with a good aim, they and their hearers benefit by them; but if their hearers mock them, they themselves benefit because they have avoided the sin of silence (in the face of error)... And so if his friends wish to be taught, let them listen, and if they are ready to mock, let them bear what is said, for teaching offered in humility to a proud mind has a grave and heavy weight.

21.2.12.en: * He says: [I ask you], showing how he speaks with humility, for he entreats persons whom pride swallows up against him, in order to bring them back to think on the teaching of the saving truth. The saints who are in the fold of the catholic Church are ready not only to teach what is true, but also to bear what is practiced against them, and they do not fear being mocked.

21.2.14.en: * Humility draws God's grace to the soul... and this frees it from these two grave pains (anger at others or the anger of others at us), for what is graver than to be angry with your brother or to anger him?! But what do I say: does humility free the soul from these two pains only? No, it frees it also from every pain (passion) and every temptation.

21.2.15.en: When St. Anthony saw the snares of Satan spread, he sighed and asked God, saying: "Who can escape them?" And God answered him: "The humble escape them... indeed they cannot even approach him."

21.2.16.en: Do you see the power of this virtue?! Truly there is nothing greater than humility, for there is nothing that can overcome it. For if some sorrows come upon a humble person, at once he blames himself that he deserves them, and does not blame others or rebuke them. And so he bears all that may surround him with complete calm, without being troubled or grieved. Thus he is not angry with anyone and angers no one.

21.2.17.en: Fr. Dorotheus If Job was not concerned that they mock him, saying: "and after I have spoken, mock on," the Apostle Paul saw his Master accept mockery and derision with joy for the salvation of the world (Lk 23:35; Heb 13:13). As he also says of Moses the prophet: "By faith Moses, when he was come to years, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter... Esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures in Egypt" (Heb 11:24, 26). And he speaks of the apostles: "as it were appointed to death: for we are made a spectacle unto the world, and to angels, and to men" (1 Cor 4:9). "Being defamed, we intreat: we are made as the filth of the world, and are the offscouring of all things unto this day" (1 Cor 4:13).

21.2.18.en: * Christ commands us to bear insults with meekness, that we may grow in virtue and put our opponents to shame (Mt 5:10-12). This is accomplished not by rebuking them but by silence.

21.2.19.en: * Paul says that the main point is not that he and his fellow apostles suffer, for this is common to all. But what is more in the apostles is that they suffer without despair or anger, but on the contrary they are filled with joy, and thereby affirm that the evils that come upon them turn to good.

21.2.20.en: St. John Chrysostom * Those who love Christ are not fools as the world thinks them (1 Cor 4:10).

21.2.21.en: Fr. Ambrosiaster As for me, is my complaint to man?

21.3.0.en: and if it were so, why should not my spirit be troubled? [4]

21.3.1.en: He assures them that he does not present his complaint to a man, because this is of no avail. Rather he presents his complaint to God, and to Him he appeals the judgment. He is the Judge and Arbiter, the searcher of hearts and reins, before whom every human being stands on an equal footing, who listens to all and cares for all.

21.3.2.en: He assures them that if his complaint were presented to a man, his spirit within him would be troubled, for a man may not care about his brother, and not perceive what is in his heart and intention, and so pass an unjust judgment. But God is longsuffering and hears man and deals with him tenderly. So the believer lifts his complaint to God, not to take vengeance on his opponents, but to please God and not men. David the prophet says: "Let the words of my mouth, and the meditation of my heart, be acceptable in thy sight, O LORD, my strength, and my redeemer" (Ps 19:14). And the Apostle Paul says: "For do I now persuade men, or God? or do I seek to please men? for if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ" (Gal 1:10).

21.3.3.en: * "For do I now persuade men, or God...? for if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ" (Gal 1:10)... Let us not think that the Apostle teaches us, by following his example, to make light of the judgments of others... But if it happens that we can please both others and God, let us please others... But by saying "now," he has included it here particularly to show that men are pleased or not pleased according to circumstances (and not according to the truth).

21.3.4.en: St. Jerome * When someone pleases others for the sake of the truth, it is the truth that is pleased, not the one who proclaimed it.

21.3.5.en: St. Augustine Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that in his rebuke of his friends, that the dialogue with them grieved his heart, so that his spirit was troubled, is a tacit confession of his human weakness. For whoever fixes his eyes on God, grief cannot creep into his heart, nor distress into his spirit. For God, the source of joy, lifts the heart above sorrows whatever their source, and grants the spirit spaciousness.

21.3.6.en: *He who seeks to please God has no ground for grief in man's displeasure with him. If, in pleasing man, he does not please God, or thinks that he does not please both God and man together, grief does not come upon him, because he has confirmed that he is a stranger to the loftiness of wisdom. Now the blessed Job confesses that he did not please God in the midst of his blows, and therefore his mind returned to grief.

21.4.0.en: Mark me, and be astonished, and lay your hand upon your mouth [5].

21.4.1.en: Whenever Job thought about his case he stood in amazement and trembling. Whenever he recalled the events that followed one another with unnatural swiftness, and the blows that came upon him from every side, trembling overtook him. He is bewildered, unable to explain what has befallen him.

21.4.2.en: *Consider what I do, and marvel at the blows I suffer. After that he says: [Put your finger on your mouth]. As though he says plainly: Since you know the good things that I practice, and see the sufferings under which I fall, take care not to sin with words because of my blows, but fear for your own wounds... Carefulness befits the fingers. Therefore it was said by the Psalmist: [Blessed be the Lord my God, who teacheth my hands to war, and my fingers to fight] (Ps 144:1). By the hands he points to work, and by the fingers to prudence.

21.4.4.en: The Church asks the people of the world to look intently at her, and not to judge her hastily, but it behooves them to think with deliberation and prudence. They see behind the Church's severe distress and the persecutions poured upon her the surpassing peace of God that fills her being, God's wonderful plan toward her, and God's work through her sufferings to fulfil her mission and her witness to His joyful Gospel. The Church asks those outside to put their hands on their mouths in amazement before the astonishing truth: God's surpassing work in His suffering Church.

21.4.5.en: * Paul says: since he is held captive by these wounds, [I bear in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus] (cf. Gal 6:17). He willingly submitted to his weaknesses in all these troubles, where the power of Christ is made perfect in virtue (cf. 2 Cor 4:10; 12:9).

21.4.6.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa * Beautiful are Paul's chains!

21.4.7.en: * He suffered for his enemies. This is the sweet-smelling offering, the acceptable sacrifice. And if you suffer for your enemies as a sweet-smelling offering, you become an acceptable sacrifice, even if you die. This is what he means by saying, be ye followers of God (Eph 5:1).

21.4.8.en: St. John Chrysostom The Fathers expanded greatly on the work of bearing sufferings, insults and mockery with joy, not only in the life of the sufferer but also in the life of the mockers themselves. St. John Chrysostom applied this to the relation of a man to his wife when she causes him sufferings, saying: [Even if it is necessary to give your life for her, do not refuse. And if it is necessary that countless troubles come upon you for her sake, and you endure all kinds of pains and troubles, do not refuse. For even if you bear all this, you have still not done what Christ did for the Church... And if you see her looking at you with disdain, constantly complaining and despising you, you can win her by your great love and tenderness toward her.]

21.5.0.en: 6 Even when I remember I am afraid, and trembling taketh hold on my flesh. 7 Wherefore do the wicked live, become old, yea, are mighty in power? 8 Their seed is established in their sight with them, and their offspring before their eyes. 9 Their houses are safe from fear, neither is the rod of God upon them. 10 Their bull gendereth, and faileth not; their cow calveth, and casteth not her calf. 11 They send forth their little ones like a flock, and their children dance. 12 They take the timbrel and harp, and rejoice at the sound of the organ. 13 They spend their days in wealth, and in a moment go down to the grave.

21.5.1.en: Even when I remember I am afraid, and trembling taketh hold on my flesh (my body was seized with trembling) [6].

21.5.2.en: Wherefore do the wicked live, become old,

21.6.1.en: The three friends expatiated on the calamities and misery that befall the wicked, but Job is amazed, and his body is seized with trembling, at what he sometimes sees of the wicked enjoying good things until they reach old age, and at the strength and authority they obtain while they are overbearing and harsh toward others.

21.6.2.en: Job does not deny that this happens to the wicked at times. They live in peace (1 Sam 25:6), and their life even extends to old age, and they have sons and grandsons, and gather huge fortunes, so that we hear in the Book of Isaiah, "the sinner being an hundred years old shall be accursed" (Isa 65:20). Not only may their lives extend to old age, but they are "mighty in power," that is, they rise to positions of authority and leadership.

21.6.3.en: Some of the wicked misunderstand God's longsuffering toward them, and Holy Scripture warns us of this: "Say not, I have sinned, and what harm hath happened unto me? for the Lord is longsuffering" (Sir 5:4). "Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering; not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance?" (Rom 2:4).

21.6.4.en: * If we do not fall under discipline and continue in our same conduct, let us use the Apostle's word that enchants us: "The goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance; but after thy hardness and impenitent heart treasurest up unto thyself wrath against the day of wrath" (Rom 2:4-5).

21.6.5.en: * "Not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance; but after thy hardness and impenitent heart treasurest up unto thyself wrath against the day of wrath" (Rom 2:4-5). Your heart has hardened like Pharaoh's heart, because your punishment has been postponed and you were not struck at once! The ten plagues were sent upon Pharaoh not as from an angry God but as from a father who warns, and the day of tenderness toward him was prolonged until he turned back from his repentance (after each plague). But punishment came upon him when he followed the people into the wilderness, and in his zeal entered the sea itself after them. This was the way by which he learned the lesson that he ought to have feared God, whom even the elements of nature obey.

21.6.6.en: St. Jerome St. Jerome uses this phrase (Rom 2:4) in reply to the followers of Pelagius to affirm God's holiness and His care for the freedom of the human will; for although God knows beforehand of the wicked man who despises His longsuffering and kindness, yet He offers him great tenderness and mercy in a longsuffering that gives him the opportunity to repent; so when the wicked man despises this, the cause is not God's foreknowledge of his contempt, but the wicked man's persistence in his wickedness.

21.6.7.en: St. Ambrose asks us not to judge people according to the good things offered them from God's mercies, who truly cares for all; for this does not mean that God does not care about their conduct, or that He does not know what they do in secret, or does not perceive what is in their consciences, but what it affirms is that with the abundance of good things granted to the wicked, they are nevertheless wretched and do not know happiness.

21.7.0.en: Their seed is established in their sight with them, and their offspring before their eyes [8].

21.7.1.en: Job points to some sinners who enjoy seeing their offspring multiply.

21.7.2.en: Often believers, and even unbelievers, are occupied with the question: Why does God allow the wicked health, long life and wealth, and also the enjoyment of power and positions of leadership? And this while they enjoy seeing their offspring share with them all these temporal blessings. For man, because of the shortness of his life, thinks that God's justice must be fulfilled in this world, and finds it hard to wait for the great day of the Lord to see divine justice fulfilled. Moreover, it is hard for the human mind to accept God's surpassing longsuffering, who waits for the wicked to turn from their wickedness and return to the divine embrace.

21.7.3.en: *Job makes this declaration to his friends: [If I suffer in this way because of my sins, why do the wicked live? They grow old in wealth also, their offspring according to their pleasure, their seed before their eyes, their houses in prosperity, no fear is in them, the rod of God does not fall upon them].

21.8.0.en: St. Ambrose Their houses are safe from fear, neither is the rod of God upon them [9].

21.8.1.en: Although Zophar pointed to the constant fears of sinners and their perpetual disquiet, Job points to some sinners who have houses safe from dangers and fears, and upon whom God does not stretch out His rod.

21.8.2.en: Since the hearts of the wicked are occupied with houses made of clay and stones, and the furnishings they hold, and the treasures stored in them, the Lord gives them the desire of their hearts, granting them temporal, transient peace, and no one approaches their possessions and treasures. But what occupies the righteous is the heavenly house and the dwellings above, and the Lord also gives them the desire of their hearts. The former receive an abundance of temporal blessings and passing security, while the latter receive an eternal inheritance that does not corrupt or perish, and an immortal heavenly glory. They rejoice, as they hear the divine voice: "I go to prepare a place for you. And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again, and receive you unto myself; that where I am, there ye may be also" (Jn 14:2-3). Therefore the Psalmist says: "He (the Lord) shall give thee the desires of thine heart" (Ps 37:4). "Thou hast given him his heart's desire, and hast not withholden the request of his lips. Selah" (Ps 21:2).

21.9.0.en: Their bull gendereth, and faileth not; their cow calveth, and casteth not her calf [10].

21.9.1.en: Some sinners are rich and their possessions increase, so that even their bulls succeed in impregnating cows so that they conceive and bear abundantly, and their animals multiply and do not die quickly of sudden diseases.

21.9.2.en: The desire of the wicked man's heart is that his animals bear many, and that there be not one miscarriage among them. But the desire of the hearts of God's children is to enjoy many children in the Lord, and that none among them be lost. They look for the day of the Lord to sing: "Behold, I and the children whom the LORD hath given me" (Isa 8:18).

21.9.3.en: Among God's children there is no barren one, but all bear twins, that is, give birth to many. For in the Apostle Peter's address on the day of Pentecost about three thousand joined the Church, who received the faith, offered repentance, and enjoyed new birth through Baptism. In one day the Apostle Peter had thousands of children whom he begot by the Gospel of Christ. And what shall we say of the Apostle Paul, who almost every day brought many into the fold of faith through his preaching with a fiery, burning heart. He does not cease to beget even in the midst of chains, so that he says of the runaway slave, the thief Onesimus: "whom I have begotten in my bonds" (Phlm 10).

21.9.4.en: If animals in Holy Scripture often point to the body, then what occupies the people of the world is bodily matters, not spiritual.

21.9.5.en: The wicked man is occupied with the birth of animals, while the true believer is occupied with the spiritual birth of human beings that they may become children of the holy God, even if the cost be chains and prison or death.

21.9.6.en: * Onesimus deserved great honor, for he was born in the very struggles of Paul, in affliction for the sake of Christ.

21.9.7.en: * Observe the burning of Paul's heart. He preached the Gospel while bound and under the lash. Oh, how blessed are the chains, how they worked with great effort in that night, and how they begot children! Truly he says of them: [I have begotten them in my bonds](أ).

21.9.8.en: Observe how Paul is glorified! He has come to have children through this way who are counted in great renown.

21.9.9.en: O the inexpressible glory of these chains, for they bestow splendor not only on those he begot, but also on those who were begotten through him in these circumstances.

21.10.0.en: St. John Chrysostom They send forth their little ones like a flock, and their children dance [11].

21.11.0.en: They take the timbrel and harp, and rejoice at the sound of the organ [12].

21.11.1.en: They live, they and their sons; the number of little children increases until they go among their neighbors like countless sheep, and the children spend their time in dancing and merriment. The elders play on musical instruments and the little ones dance. The fathers are not concerned with their children's walking in the way of the Lord, as Abraham commanded his children (Gen 18:19), nor do they urge them to worship God, but all that concerns them is amusement, revelry and the enjoyment of temporal pleasures.

21.11.2.en: St. John Chrysostom often warned parents against neglect in the upbringing of their children, showing how grave this sin is, which he reckons one of the extremely grave sins, so that he did not hesitate to call it child-murder.

21.11.3.en: * The corruption of children does not come from nothing, but from the madness that seizes fathers regarding earthly concerns. Concern for earthly things alone, and counting everything else of no value, drives them involuntarily to neglect the souls of their children. I say, these fathers (and let no one think that these words arise in me from anger) are worse than murderers of children. The first separates the body from the soul, but the other casts both together into the fires of Gehenna. Death is inevitable according to the natural order, but the second fate parents could avoid if the parents' neglect did not lead to it. Bodily death can end in a moment by the resurrection when it comes, but there is no reward awaiting the lost soul. It does not enjoy the resurrection, but suffers eternal pains. This means that it is not unjust to call these fathers worse than murderers of children. It is not as cruel to sharpen a sword and hold it in the right hand to plunge it into a child's heart as it is to destroy and humiliate the soul, for there is nothing equal to the soul.

21.11.4.en: St. John Chrysostom The wicked think that they enjoy life because of the multitude of their children, without caring about their conduct and inner life and enjoyment of eternal glory. But the righteous feel that they, with their families, are surrounded by the saints like a light heavenly cloud, having fellowship with the Fathers, prophets, apostles, martyrs and all believers, whether those who have departed or their contemporaries, and even having fellowship with the heavenly orders. Their life is an unceasing heavenly feast and a joyful festival on a surpassing level! Their hearts and thoughts become strings of spiritual harps, upon which the Holy Spirit of God plays, so that heaven rejoices, and the heavenly ones rejoice with songs of spiritual joy.

21.11.5.en: They spend their days in wealth,

21.12.0.en: and in a moment go down to the grave [13].

21.12.1.en: With all this they are prosperous, spending their days in the ease of life; poverty has no place among them.

21.12.2.en: As for the fruit of their wickedness, in a moment they go down to the grave, without warning. Perhaps he means that at times in their death they do not suffer from incurable diseases and pains, but in a moment they die and go down to the tomb. As the Psalmist says: "For yet a little while, and the wicked shall not be: yea, thou shalt diligently consider his place, and it shall not be" (Ps 37:10). As the wise man says: "As the whirlwind passeth, so is the wicked no more: but the righteous is an everlasting foundation" (Prov 10:25).

21.12.3.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that the speech here does not necessarily mean the falling of the wicked in a moment, and their collapse, and the loss of their temporal goods, but it may mean that what they enjoy in this world, however long their life, they enjoy as for a moment, where the whole of life passes in a moment, and they find themselves before the Judge, having prepared for themselves the way of Hades or eternal Gehenna.

21.12.4.en: *Yes, blessed one, you have described their delights at length. How do you now declare that in a moment they go down to the grave, except because all this long time of their present life is known to be but a moment when it reaches its end.

21.13.s.en: 3. The wicked's misuse of good things

21.13.0.en: 14 Therefore they say unto God, Depart from us; for we desire not the knowledge of thy ways. 15 What is the Almighty, that we should serve him? and what profit should we have, if we pray unto him? 16 Lo, their good is not in their hand: the counsel of the wicked is far from me.

21.13.1.en: Therefore they say unto God, Depart from us;

21.13.2.en: for we desire not the knowledge of thy ways [14].

21.13.3.en: The wicked misuse all that has been given them of wealth, authority or success, and it reaches the point of their challenging God Himself and rejecting the commandment. They are terrified at the presence of God. "They say to God: Depart from us." They do not wish to trouble themselves with being under His eyes, and do not want fear of Him to turn them aside from their thinking. They feel that they have no need of Him, and reject His knowledge in which they find no pleasure, for His knowledge rebukes them for their rebellion, and as the Lord Christ says: "And this is the condemnation, that light is come into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light, because their deeds were evil. For every one that doeth evil hateth the light, neither cometh to the light, lest his deeds should be reproved" (Jn 3:19-20). And on the day of the Lord, the Lord gives them the desire of their hearts, saying to them: [Depart from me... for I know you not] (Mt 25:41). For whoever cannot bear to see God by faith here in this world will not be able to bear seeing Him on the day of judgment. [They shall say to the mountains, Fall on us; and to the hills, Cover us from the face of him that sitteth on the throne] (Hos 10:8; Lk 23:30). "They shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him" (Zech 12:10).

21.13.4.en: The whole being of the true believer rejoices at seeing the One he longed to meet face to face (1 Cor 13:12), but the wicked man cannot bear to stay before God, but his works bring him out to the outer darkness.

21.13.5.en: The wicked are not pleased with the knowledge of God's ways, and God is not pleased with the ways of the wicked. For darkness cannot endure light, and light takes no pleasure in darkness. As the Apostle Paul says: "For what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness?" (2 Cor 6:14)

21.13.6.en: * "They say to God: Depart from us!" Even fools do not dare to say this in words, and yet all the wicked say to God by their conduct, not by their words: "Depart from us." For those who practice works that God the Almighty forbids, what do they do but shut themselves against the Almighty? As thinking on His commandments is God's entering into man, so resisting His commandments is keeping God from dwelling in the heart...

21.13.7.en: [For we desire not the knowledge of thy ways], thus it is: they do not care to seek His knowledge.

21.13.8.en: The Truth says: [And that servant, which knew his lord's will, and prepared not himself, neither did according to his will, shall be beaten with many stripes. But he that knew not, and did commit things worthy of stripes, shall be beaten with few stripes] (Lk 12:47-48). Some choose not to know what they ought to do, and think they will be beaten less if they are ignorant of what they ought to do.

21.13.9.en: But not to know something is one thing, and for a man to choose not to know is another thing. For some wish to know but are unable; these do not know. But he who turns his ear away from the voice of truth lest he know, such a one is not in ignorance but is a despiser.

21.13.10.en: Now God's "way" is peace, God's way is humility, God's way is longsuffering. But the wicked care for none of this, and say: "We desire not the knowledge of thy ways." They exalt themselves in pride in this life. They are swallowed up in honors, that they may possess them, for they covet them. They ignore God's ways in the thoughts of their hearts.

21.13.12.en: * He who sits in darkness at night does not run after the light of the sun as long as he does not see it. But when dawn comes and the splendor of the sun begins to shine upon him, at once he follows its light.

21.13.13.en: St. John Chrysostom * "For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face" (1 Cor 13:12). This is what the angels, who are called our angels, actually see. They are our angels in the sense that as soon as we are delivered from the power of darkness, we receive the earnest of the Spirit and are translated into the kingdom of Christ, and begin to be related to the angels.

21.14.0.en: St. Augustine What is the Almighty, that we should serve him? and what profit should we have, if we pray unto him? [15].

21.14.1.en: With unseemly boldness they protest against Him saying: "What is the Almighty, that we should serve him? and what profit should we have, if we pray unto him?" They imitate Pharaoh who said: "Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice?" (Ex 5:2) They see in God an unknown personage to whom some ascribe power though in their view he is of no use, so they do not want him to have anything to do with them, nor do they want anything to do with him.

21.14.2.en: They look at worship as a duty hard to bear, or as a kind of grievous servitude, as they ask: "that we should serve him?" They see themselves as strong, mighty masters who do not accept submission to God: "Wherefore say my people, We are lords; we will come no more unto thee?" (Jer 2:31).

21.14.3.en: They say: "It is vain to serve God: and what profit is it that we have kept his ordinance..." (Mal 3:13-14), so there is no need to resort to God, for prayer in their view is of no use, but is a waste of time and energy.

21.14.4.en: The wicked may perceive in their minds God's power, and know the possibility of His working in the lives of men, but through their enjoyment of bodily pleasures and their preoccupation with the delights of the world they quiet their consciences by claiming that God ignores mankind and does not perceive their true needs, so that He appears as one in weakness and powerless to support them. Moreover, time is precious to them for gathering wealth and obtaining temporal honors, the object of their love. All worship of God, in their view, is a waste of time. And they murmur because God often postpones answering their requests until He grants them what, according to His divine mind, they are to possess, He who is the Creator of all gifts and good things.

21.14.5.en: * When man's mind turns miserably outward, he is immersed in the pleasures of bodily things, and does not return to his depths, nor can he think of the Invisible One... So it is written: "The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God" (Ps 14:1; 53:1)...

21.14.6.en: It often happens that people make it their aim to serve their fellow creatures whom they see with the bodily eye rather than to serve God whom they do not see. For in all they do they reach out as far as their eyes reach, and since they cannot reach God with their eyes, they either make light of rendering allegiance to Him, or if they begin to do so they are filled with anxiety...

21.14.7.en: But when what is visible is withdrawn from before them... the eyes of the body are indeed open but they cannot see or perceive... The sense of patience departs from them, because the One who dwelt in them has left them, and the house of the body remained empty. The invisible spirit that was accustomed to see through the windows of the body has departed.

21.14.8.en: Therefore the invisible things are better than the visible. It befits all the carnal to come to a decision for themselves, and by the ladder of contemplation to ascend to God. He is God in that He remains invisible, and the Most High continues where He cannot be comprehended. But there are some who do not doubt that God exists and that He cannot be comprehended, but they ask things of Him and do not seek Him, but seek His external gifts.

21.14.9.en: [And what profit shall we have if we pray to Him]. During prayer, if God Himself is not the object of our petition, the mind is at once disturbed in prayer... God longs to be Himself the beloved more than the things He created, and for eternal things to be sought, not temporary ones. As it is written: "But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you" (Mt 6:33).

21.14.11.en: Lo, their good is not in their hand:

21.15.0.en: the counsel of the wicked is far from me [16].

21.15.1.en: They will not accept the belief that what is in their hands is God's gift to them, but think it made by their hands, the fruit of their toil, intelligence and planning. Thus they close their hearts to their needy brethren, reckoning that giving to them is a plundering of their possessions and a squandering of what they labored for. They hold fast to what they have lest they lose the goods from their hands.

21.15.2.en: *The rich man usually imagines that he commits no sin as long as he does not rob the poor materially. But the sin of the rich lies in his not sharing his wealth with the poor. The rich man's keeping all his wealth means in fact committing a kind of theft. The real reason is that all riches are from God, so it belongs to all equally... And the proof of this surrounds us everywhere.

21.15.3.en: Look at the fresh fruit that the trees and thickets produce.

21.15.4.en: Look at the fertile soil that gives every year an abundant harvest like this.

21.15.5.en: Look at the sweet grapes on the clusters that give us wine to drink...

21.15.6.en: Perhaps the rich claim that they own much land where fruits and grain grow, but it is God who makes the seed sprout and ripen. So it is the duty of the rich to share every harvest of their land with all who work in it, and with all who have need.

21.15.7.en: St. John Chrysostom They pass this spirit on to their offspring and their friends, who walk in the same direction, but Job declares: "the counsel of the wicked is far from me."

21.16.0.en: 17 How oft is the candle of the wicked put out! and how oft cometh their destruction upon them! God distributeth sorrows in his anger. 18 They are as stubble before the wind, and as chaff that the storm carrieth away. 19 God layeth up his iniquity for his children: he rewardeth him, and he shall know it. 20 His eyes shall see his destruction, and he shall drink of the wrath of the Almighty. 21 For what pleasure hath he in his house after him, when the number of his months is cut off in the midst?

21.16.1.en: How oft is the candle of the wicked put out! and how oft cometh their destruction upon them! God distributeth sorrows in his anger [17].

21.16.2.en: Since Job spoke at length of the wicked's success in this world, he returns to ask: [How oft is the candle of the wicked put out?] Do you not see it often burning until the wick has burned out, and after that going out of itself?

21.16.3.en: How often do you see that [their destruction comes upon them, or that God distributes sorrows to them in His anger?] Do you not see that often their joys and luxury continued to the end?

21.16.4.en: * The righteous dies in the strength of his simplicity, and in full mastery of his will, having a soul full as if of meadows. But the sinner, though in luxurious living, with sweet perfumes rising from him, closes his life in the bitterness of his soul, and passes his last day without taking anything of the good things he once enjoyed, carrying nothing but the wages of his wickedness.

21.16.5.en: *The holy Job answers: Do not think that you are happy while immersed in pleasures because God's blows have not come upon you in this life. [The candle of the wicked is put out]. It gives light for a time, but does not bear eternal light. And although the world favors such people because they practice the will of the ruler of the world(ب) (Jn 14:30), yet generally there comes a moment of turning in events, when sorrows come from the wrath and displeasure of heaven, when the wicked are sifted "as stubble before the wind." The unjust are sifted as chaff, and the righteous as wheat. Look to the Lord who said to Peter: "Behold, Satan hath desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat: but I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not" (Lk 22:31-32).

21.16.6.en: St. Ambrose The believer cherishes the word of God as the lamp that lights his way, through which he passes into the Father's bosom to enjoy glories on an eternal level. But the wicked man sees in wealth or authority or the enjoyment of bodily pleasures his lamp that drives him not to the kingdom of light but is a lamp that leads him astray and brings him into the kingdom of darkness. And as the Apostle Paul says that even Satan is transformed into an angel of light, to deceive believers, perhaps to hold them captive under his authority, so that they become children of darkness.

21.16.7.en: But the deceptions of the enemy of good will not stand before men of faith but are dispersed, as a lamp is put out!

21.16.8.en: *The wicked man often thinks that earthly resources are to him like a great lamp is to light, but when destruction comes upon him he loses the wealth he loved more than himself.

21.17.0.en: They are as stubble before the wind, and as chaff that the storm carrieth away [18].

21.17.1.en: Job holds that his speaking of the wicked's success does not mean that they are truly successful, for they are as stubble before the wind, and as chaff that the storm carrieth away. They are trifling, losing all value, prepared for destruction, and are exposed to it at the height of their glory and might.

21.17.2.en: *When the wicked man is seen in strength, and when he is like one who has no restraint or opponent to his violent deeds, the weak count him as ballast (a weight used to balance a ship or a balloon), and as rooted in this world. But when the firm judgment comes from the Judge, [the wicked shall be as stubble before the wind]... [and as ashes that the whirlwind scatters]. The life of the wicked man in the eyes of the Almighty is like ashes, which may seem green for a moment, but is seen as having been scattered by the divine judgment, left aside for eternal burning. These ashes the whirlwind scatters. In this "our God shall come, and shall not keep silence: a fire shall devour before him, and it shall be very tempestuous round about him" (Ps 50:3).

21.17.4.en: The wind, without which trees cannot deepen their roots and multiply their fruits, is the very same that scatters the stubble and strews the chaff, so that it has no place of rest. What builds the believer shatters the wicked.

21.17.5.en: If the wind points to the Holy Spirit, then the Holy Spirit by whom the birth of believers as children of God is accomplished in the waters of Baptism, and by whom they are renewed until they truly become the icon of Christ, is the same fiery Holy Spirit before whom the thorns of sin cannot stand, but are burned!
